---
title: "Plugin developer SDK"
---

The SDK gives you a small starting point to develop a BenchWeave device plugin with AI: **generate, implement, test, review, then prepare a release**. Use this guide for SDK installation, project generation, testing and packaging. The [device developer guide](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave/blob/main/docs/device-developer-guide.md) (main repository) covers device evidence, integration requirements, firmware and qualification.

The device is the hardware. The plugin is its Python integration and descriptor. Follow the [developer directory convention](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave/blob/main/docs/device-developer-guide.md#repository-layout-for-device-plugins): `plugins/<manufacturer>/<name>/`, with `src/<python_package>/` inside that project. The name normally identifies the device model, such as `fnirsi/dps150`.

The current SDK is `benchweave-sdk` 0.7.1 for Python 3.13+, OTDP 0.2.2 and adapter API 1.1, with registry 0.1.2 schemas. Its source lives in this repository. The [main BenchWeave repository](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave) mounts it at `packages/sdk`. Build it separately from the gateway. It supplies structural typing interfaces, offline contract validation, a scripted mock host, bounded async conformance helpers, an external project generator and file-inventory helpers.

## 1. Install the SDK and generate your project

Install the SDK from PyPI:

```sh
# plugin authoring: `new` renders the copier template (issue #347 WS2)
pip install 'benchweave-sdk[scaffold]'
# scaffold-free install (check/conformance/preview only)
pip install benchweave-sdk
# or as an isolated CLI tool
uv tool install benchweave-sdk
```

For the newest unreleased code, install from the default branch:

```sh
pip install git+https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave-sdk.git
```

Full channel list: see the README Installation section.

PyPI is the default install channel: `pip install benchweave-sdk` or `uv pip install benchweave-sdk`. Contributors and maintainers can instead build from a checkout of the main BenchWeave repository. Run this from that checkout's root. `packages/sdk` is the submodule mount path there, not a directory in this repository:

```sh
uv build packages/sdk --out-dir dist/sdk
```

In your development directory, create an environment. Then install the built wheel from the checkout's `dist/sdk/`:

```sh
uv venv --python 3.13
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install 'dist/sdk/benchweave_sdk-*.whl[scaffold]'
benchweave-sdk new plugins/acme/model100 --package benchweave_acme_model100
cd plugins/acme/model100
uv pip install -e '.[test]'
pytest
```

Keep the environment that contains the SDK wheel. If you create a new environment inside the project, install the wheel there too. For a repeatable `uv lock` against a locally built wheel, configure that wheel or your organisation's package source explicitly.

Run `benchweave-sdk doctor` from the project to compare the pin with the installed SDK. The command names the recorded version, the installed version, and the reinstall command when they differ. The command works offline and does not fail the run. A stale SDK is a report, not an error.

The generated project also carries `.copier-answers.yml` at its root: the durable provenance record of which SDK template version produced it (`new` pins the canonical repository and the matching `v<version>` template tag — template version == SDK version). The pyproject pin that `doctor` reads remains a mutable declaration the author may move; the answers file is the record.

Moving a project to a newer template: `benchweave-sdk upgrade` (from the project root, on a committed and clean git tree) fetches the installed SDK's released template tag from the canonical repository and applies it — author-owned files (pyproject, README, CLAUDE.md, `src/<pkg>/**`, `tests/**`) are preserved byte-for-byte; the managed `AI-GUIDE.md` moves with the template, and a file you both changed gets conflict markers to resolve and commit. Released template tags only: a development install's version has no tag and the update refuses with `upgrade_tag_missing`. Projects scaffolded before the copier port gain provenance with `benchweave-sdk adopt` — it infers the package name and base version from the generated `pyproject.toml` (`--package` / `--scaffolded-at` override) and refuses a project whose provenance it cannot establish.

Replace `acme/model100` with your manufacturer and device or plugin name. The destination controls the directory hierarchy. The `--package` option controls the Python import package. The SDK creates missing parent directories and refuses to overwrite an existing project. A destination that you reach through a symlinked directory is canonicalized before any write. On macOS, `/tmp/...` is such a symlink. Messages report the real path.

```text
plugins/
└── acme/
    └── model100/                       # Independent build/test/release root
        ├── pyproject.toml
        ├── README.md
        ├── AI-GUIDE.md
        ├── CLAUDE.md                   # Agent notes; root dev tooling
        ├── AGENTS.md                   # SDK-managed agent guide; CLAUDE.md imports it
        ├── .claude/skills/             # Five SDK-managed workflow skills
        ├── src/benchweave_acme_model100/
        │   ├── __init__.py
        │   ├── adapter.py
        │   ├── protocol.py
        │   ├── descriptor.json
        │   ├── protocol.md
        │   ├── vectors.json
        │   └── skills/                 # Seeded agent skills; ship in the wheel
        │       ├── develop-plugin/SKILL.md
        │       └── drive-device/SKILL.md
        └── tests/test_plugin.py
```

The root also carries `AGENTS.md`, the SDK-managed agent guide: `CLAUDE.md` imports it, and `benchweave-sdk upgrade` refreshes it together with the five workflow skills under `.claude/skills/` (`benchweave-plugin-workflow`, `benchweave-descriptor`, `benchweave-plugin-ui`, `benchweave-adapter-testing`, `benchweave-capture`). They are repo-level dev tooling outside `src/<python_package>/`; they never enter the plugin wheel. The seeded package skills inside `src/<python_package>/skills/` are different content and do ship in the wheel. If you edit a managed file, the upgrade writes conflict markers; resolve both sides, then commit. A project made before these files existed adds the `@AGENTS.md` import line to its `CLAUDE.md` by hand.

Generate the dependency lock and retain it. Add your chosen licence file. When you develop custom firmware, add `firmware/` with its own build and tests. The starter does not create these project-specific files. You can copy the manufacturer and name directory into its own external repository unchanged. It has no runtime dependency on BenchWeave core or the SDK. The SDK is a development dependency.

The starter deliberately implements a made-up, read-only identify and voltage protocol. A pass of its tests demonstrates that the tools work. It says nothing about your instrument.

## 2. Give the AI the facts and prompts

Open the generated **`AI-GUIDE.md`**. It contains five copyable prompts: establish device facts, implement with mocks, demonstrate behaviour, prepare independent review, and prepare release artefacts for owner review.

Provide the exact model, firmware, transport, supported operations and authoritative protocol evidence. Review the AI's proposed scope before you replace the example. The AI should keep the protocol code separate from the async adapter. The AI should use only the supplied scoped host services. The current gateway loader supports package-relative and standard-library imports. Arbitrary third-party runtime dependencies need more integration work.

For custom hardware, follow [Build my own device firmware](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave/blob/main/docs/develop-your-device.md) (main repository) as well. Firmware and the Python plugin have separate builds and compatibility evidence, even when you maintain them in one project.

## 3. Run the checks

From your plugin project, use the environment that contains the SDK:

```sh
pytest
benchweave-sdk check src/benchweave_acme_model100/descriptor.json
uv build
```

Generated tests cover identify and read, quiet lifecycle, invalid inputs, pre-dispatch cancellation and expiry, and uncertain malformed and transport responses. Extend them for your actual operations, failure modes and evidence. `check_operation` validates request and result schemas and correlation. `check_lifecycle` checks a quiet lifecycle and repeated cleanup. Both bound cooperative async calls with a configurable wall-clock timeout. Python that blocks, or code that suppresses cancellation, needs process-level isolation.

Descriptor checks currently cover its schema, matching capabilities and policies, unique parameter names, ordered ranges and transport-provider declarations (next subsection). These are **partial checks**, not all S01–S18, C01–C12 or M01–M14 obligations. The SDK provides no physical transport provider, complete profile or capture test harness, or hardware qualification certificate.

### Standards versions: per-pin validation and the served set {#per-pin-standards}

The SDK does not validate against "the" OTDP schema. It vendors a **multi-version standards tree**. It validates every document against its descriptor's **own pinned version**. The `otdp_version` field decides which bytes answer. A 0.2.0-pinned descriptor validates against 0.2.0's schemas. A 0.2.2-pinned descriptor validates against 0.2.2's schemas. Neither is reinterpreted through the active version. Explicit `otdp/<version>/<file>` lookup keys resolve the same way.

`standards-lock.json` pins what the SDK carries: one row per retained, in-range `(id, version)`, with yanked-in-interval versions carried but marked. The lock also carries a verbatim mirror of the gateway's `dependency_policy` block. The mirror holds the declared ranges, yank records and retirements. Every vendored file is sha256-checked against its lock row at load. `benchweave-sdk sync-standards --check` re-verifies the committed tree, the stamps and the row-marker and mirror agreement offline, with no gateway checkout.

Pin classification follows that state, under stable refusal prefixes:

- `version_not_served:` means that this SDK does not carry the pin. The pin is out of the declared range or was never retained here. The refusal carries the five VR-37 fields: standard, pinned version, supported range, nearest move-to and the migration-note pointer.
- `retired_identifier:` means that the pin names a retired version. A retired version was used, is now dead, and will never be reissued.
- A **yanked** pin is carried and yank-marked. It stays conforming and validates against its own bytes. A deprecation warning names the derived **move-to**. The move-to is the highest served version. When nothing is served, the declared range's lower bound is the guidance. When the pin orders above every served version, the move-to is a downgrade. The warning then carries the exact text ` (a downgrade — no served version is newer)`. It does not present the move-to as an upgrade path.

### Transport providers (custom transports) {#transport-providers}

A `custom` transport may declare a pinned **transport-provider contract** (OTDP 0.2.1). The declaration is an optional `provider` object on the transport. It carries the required `feature_id` and an `{id, path, sha256}` pin to the reviewed contract document inside your plugin package. `benchweave-sdk check` verifies the whole declaration offline. It refuses with named, machine-matchable prefixes:

- `provider_feature_missing:` means that the provider's `feature_id` is not in `required_features`.
- `provider_transport_undeclared:` means that an `otdp.transport.*` feature is required but no provider on the custom transport declares it. It also fires when the provider's `feature_id` is not a sanctioned `otdp.transport.<name>/<semver>` id. Such a declaration is one that nothing admissible can ever back.
- `unknown_otdp_feature:` means an `otdp.*` feature id that is neither corpus-known nor declared through a provider. The namespace is corpus-owned. A typo or a fake version does not pass.
- `provider_contract_missing:` means that the pin does not resolve to a contained regular file. Provider pins are **descriptor-relative**: the contract ships beside your descriptor, and subdirectories are allowed. Provider pins refuse traversal, absolute paths and symlinked components.
- `provider_contract_hash_mismatch:` means that the pinned bytes do not hash to the pinned `sha256`.
- `provider_contract_invalid:` means that the pinned document fails one of these checks: the transport-provider contract schema; grammar subschemas that are not valid Draft 2020-12 schemas; kinds that are not unique strings; a kind that shadows a generic transfer kind; identity fields that disagree, including disagreement with the descriptor's own declaration.

A provider in the wrong place refuses through the ordinary error surface for schema validation. The wrong places are a non-custom transport and the missing adapter integration mode. Provider-object shape faults refuse through the same surface. A `custom` transport **without** a provider stays valid. That is the honestly-incomplete posture, not a refusal. The Python entry points behind these checks are `validation.validate_transport_provider` (contract documents) and `validation.verify_provider_pin` (pin resolution).

These checks prove the declaration **well-formed and self-consistent** only. Only the gateway can prove the grant: that your host admitted the pinned contract and that `connection_key` resolves to a connection it backs. An offline pass is not an admission claim.

## Local UI preview (simulated)

[`benchweave-sdk check-ui`](../reference/cli/check_ui.qmd) and [`check-preset`](../reference/cli/check_preset.qmd) validate presentation candidates offline. [`preview-ui`](../reference/cli/preview_ui.qmd) previews a plugin project. It serves the standalone host on the scripted mock transport, on loopback only. The command needs the `[server]` extra. On a default installation, it refuses with `benchweave_sdk_server_extras_missing:` and exit 2. `preview-ui` never leaves the mock transport. Every scenario, observation and control receipt is simulated and labelled as such. The preview path has no gateway, registry or hardware reach. The served document's shape is pinned by [plugin-ui-preview-v1](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave/blob/main/standards/plugin-ui-preview-v1/preview-document.schema.json) (main repository). The emitter validates it. The `renderer_version` field of the served document reports the version of the SDK that emitted it. Previews render the manifest's declared plots and channel hints from per-scenario snapshot values. Each observed target gets one simulated value. Previews do not show observation history.

For real hardware, use `benchweave-sdk-server serve --transport serial` directly. The command starts without a device path. Scan from the index page, then bind one listed port with its Bind button. Bind and Unbind need the operator action token. `serve` prints this token at startup. The launch URL carries it. The command also writes it to `operator-action-token.json` under the capture root. The binding is stored in `device-bindings.json` under the working directory. Name another file with `--bindings <path>` or `BENCHWEAVE_STANDALONE_BINDINGS`. The stored binding survives a restart: the next serve connects to the bound port without a device path. A connect refuses `not_ready` with reason `binding_stale` when the bound port is gone. The device page shows a re-pick action beside this refusal. A bind also refuses when the picked port is no longer present, or when the port now carries a different USB serial than the scan recorded. Scan again, then pick one of the listed ports. A connect also refuses when the unit answers the identify request with a different manufacturer or model than the descriptor declares. The session stays closed. Pass `--device <path>` for the headless form. The host then serves that constant path. The bindings file is still opened and validated at startup. The stored binding is not consulted to resolve the endpoint in this form. The pick flow in the UI can still write the file.

The SDK's runtime dependencies are Click, jsonschema (with the referencing, rfc3339-validator and rfc3987 format backends) and Rich. This repository's `pyproject.toml` declares them all. In a main-checkout layout, the file is at `packages/sdk/pyproject.toml`. The wheel vendors the canonical contract JSONs and the pure presentation validator.

Operational notes: `preview-ui` is an interactive tool. It serves until you interrupt it, by design. It exits 0 on SIGINT as a normal stop. The default port is 8477. Pass `--port` to change it.

::: {.callout-caution}
Under the explicitly acknowledged `--allow-network` mode, request bodies have no handler timeout. Only untrusted peers are affected. Do not expose the preview to untrusted peers.
:::

## Mock transports (offline rehearsal)

The standalone host serves a plugin on a scripted mock transport when you run `serve --transport mock` or `preview-ui`. For `serve`, the `mock` transport is the default. The script comes from the evidence file of the plugin, `src/<package>/vectors.json`. The file declares which of the two transaction dialects the adapter uses. The host serves the mock that matches the dialect.

**The two dialects.** Declare the dialect with the file-level `transaction_dialect` key. If you omit the key, the file is a `stream_exchange` script. Every row is a `{"request": ..., "response": ...}` pair of strings. The mock serves whole-dict exchanges. This is the shape of the starter protocol. The request is `ID?\n` and the response is one line.

If you declare `"transaction_dialect": "send_receive"`, the rows form a binary section 8.1 SEND/RECEIVE conversation. The strings of each row are frames. The `stream_send` of the adapter must match the next scripted request frame exactly. The mock serves `stream_receive` with the exact outcomes of the serial backend. The section "A standalone runtime around the writer" below states these outcomes.

**Encoding.** By default, the bytes of a row are the ASCII bytes of the row string. Set `"encoding": "hex"` at file level, or on one row, for binary frames. A string is then a hex byte string, for example `"response": "53544154000a"`. The `ascii` encoding refuses a string that is not ASCII. The `hex` encoding refuses an odd-length string or a non-hex string. Both refusals give the row.

**The row contract.** Every row carries a `response`. A row without `request` is a response-only row. A response-only row is a device-initiated frame that the mock releases to the inbound stream. The release happens in row order, when the conversation reaches the row. Response-only rows need `transaction_dialect: "send_receive"`. The default dialect cannot contain an unsolicited frame.

A row can also carry a `name`. Diagnostics refer to a row by its `name` or by its index.

**How selection works.** The host reads the declaration at connect time and builds the matching mock host. Nothing else changes. `serve --transport serial` never reads `vectors.json`. The script is rehearsal evidence, not device configuration.

**How the script loops.** The mock detects a repeating unit from the captured rows. The rows before the first full unit are the establishment. The mock serves these rows once. The unit then serves every later cycle in captured order.

A capture needs at least two full units of evidence. A capture with no derivable unit is not an error. Two causes are usual. A truncated capture is one cause. A polled value that varies across occurrences of the same request is another cause. Such a capture then obeys the plain tail rule. Under this rule, row 0 is the establishment. The whole tail becomes the cycle. The cycle repeats in captured order on every restore.

A repeating unit must contain at least one row with a `request`. A response-only row releases once per cycle pass. A captured burst drains once. Then the line goes quiet. When the adapter consumes a row with a `request`, the cycle re-arms.

**What the mock can and cannot rehearse.** The `send_receive` mock reproduces exactly the RECEIVE outcomes of the serial backend: `exact_bytes` precedence over `termination`, the `lf` and `crlf` terminators, the overlong-line discard, the quiet-line `{"data": b""}`, and a partial frame retained across a deadline. The mock releases unsolicited frames strictly in row order. The mock cannot rehearse the interleaving that a real streaming device produces between rows. The mock does not serve `can_receive`, `can_send`, `i2c_transfer` or `spi_transfer`. A plugin that needs those kinds needs a real transport.

The timings of the mock are not the timings of the device. The quiet line answers at once, not after the quiet window of the backend. A receive that cannot complete raises the `TimeoutError` of the backend at once. The mock does not wait until the deadline.

For this reason, a rehearsal proves the command flow, not the timing budget. A capture that fits its `timeout_ms` on the mock proves nothing about the hardware budget. Budget-fit evidence needs `--transport serial` and the device.

**The bound, in simple words.** The discipline of the mock is exact. When a frame that the adapter SENDs differs from the frame of the scripted row, the rehearsal fails. The failure gives the row and both frames. The mock never guesses what the device meant.

But a script can prove only what its rows record. A script that does not match the real device proves nothing about the device. Use `--transport serial` and the hardware for interleaving, for non-serial transports, for timing, and for any claim about the device.

## Capture without a gateway (standalone writer)

Plugin and bench development happens on machines that never run the gateway. `benchweave_sdk.capture.StandaloneCaptureWriter` implements the three capture methods that an adapter calls in gateway mode: `artifact_append`, `artifact_finalise` and `artifact_abort`. The writer works over one directory per capture on a local filesystem. It is three of the eight `CaptureServices` members. Device I/O still comes from a transport that a composing runtime supplies.

```python
from benchweave_sdk.capture import StandaloneCaptureWriter

writer = StandaloneCaptureWriter()          # or StandaloneCaptureWriter(some_path)
await writer.artifact_append("cap-demo-1", chunk, context)
manifest = await writer.artifact_finalise("cap-demo-1", {
    "format": "waveform_f64le",
    "started_at": "2026-09-22T00:00:00Z",
    "sample_count": 1024, "sample_interval_s": 0.001, "unit": "V",
}, context)
```

The capture root is an explicit constructor argument. Next comes the `BENCHWEAVE_CAPTURE_DIR` environment variable. Last comes `captures/` under the current working directory. A relative root resolves against the working directory when you construct the writer.

The writer refuses a root inside the installed package tree. A reinstall or upgrade wipes such a root, and the SDK's inventory verification refuses unlisted files. The writer also refuses a `BENCHWEAVE_CAPTURE_DIR` that is set but empty or whitespace-only. It also refuses a root that exists but is not a directory.

::: {.callout-caution}
A reinstall or an upgrade deletes a capture root inside the installed package tree. Do not put the capture root there.
:::

Each capture event is one directory. The directory holds `manifest.json`, a `staging/` tree while chunks accumulate, the primary artefact, and an optional `renderings/` tree that the plugin writes itself. The primary artefact name depends on the format: `<capture_id>.f64` for `waveform_f64le`, `.bin` for `raw_binary`, `.csv`, `.txt` or `.vcd` for declared extension formats, and `.data` otherwise.

The manifest's `sha256`, `byte_length` and `artifact_id` (`art-<sha256>`) are computed over the real published bytes. Standalone extras live under `x-standalone-*` keys. The finalise format must be in the constructor's declared set. The set comes from `formats=`, and it holds the two core formats by default. An empty set refuses everything. The writer refuses a capture that appended nothing. It does not publish an empty capture. It also refuses a `waveform_f64le` capture whose byte length is not `sample_count` × 8, as the gateway refuses that too. An abort deletes only `staging/` and the in-flight primary. A published capture and `renderings/` survive an unconditional `finally`-cleanup abort.

Standalone does not apply the gateway's two host-side admission checks: the descriptor's `capture_limits` (G2) and the host's storage quota (G3). A capture that finalises standalone can still be refused by a gateway.

There is no automatic import of standalone captures into the gateway. Ingest is a separate, deliberate path.

### A standalone runtime around the writer (worked example)

The writer is three of the eight members. A bench script that drives an adapter without a gateway needs the other five as well: clocks, evidence, and the transport. The example below is one complete `CaptureServices` object for a device on a serial port. A contributor fork of the ADC board wrote a serial host for the same purpose, and this example is adapted from it.

It implements the three scoped stream transactions of OTDP §8.1 exactly. It adds one behaviour that the spec leaves unspecified: the quiet-line answer below. The transactions are `stream_send`, `stream_receive` and `stream_exchange`. In them, `exact_bytes` takes precedence over `termination`. Only `lf` and `crlf` terminators exist here, because serial has no `eom`. Unspecified fields are refused. An incomplete frame is never returned as complete.

A receive that sees no bytes at all for a short quiet window answers `{"data": b""}`. Nothing was offered. Adapters read that as a quiet line, not as an error. The DPS-150 plugin's telemetry drain ends on exactly that answer. Once a frame starts, it is only ever returned whole. Bytes already read when a deadline expires stay buffered for the next receive, so a slow reply is not lost.

The capture methods delegate to `StandaloneCaptureWriter`. This is author-side tooling, not an SDK module. Copy it into your project and adapt it.

```python
import asyncio
import json
import time
from datetime import UTC, datetime
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from benchweave_sdk.capture import StandaloneCaptureWriter

_TERMINATORS = {"lf": b"\n", "crlf": b"\r\n"}
_RECEIVE = {"max_bytes", "termination", "exact_bytes"}
_FIELDS = {
    "stream_send": {"kind", "data"},
    "stream_receive": {"kind"} | _RECEIVE,
    "stream_exchange": {"kind", "data"} | _RECEIVE,
}


class BenchContext:
    """A minimal OperationContext for bench use: identity, deadline, cancellation."""

    def __init__(self, operation_id: str, timeout_s: float,
                 dataset_id: str | None = None) -> None:
        self.operation_id = operation_id
        self.dataset_id = dataset_id
        self.deadline_monotonic = time.monotonic() + timeout_s
        self.dispatched = False
        self._cancelled = False

    def cancel(self) -> None:
        self._cancelled = True

    def is_cancelled(self) -> bool:
        return self._cancelled

    async def mark_dispatch_started(self) -> None:
        self.dispatched = True


class SerialStandaloneHost:
    """All eight CaptureServices members over one serial port, without a gateway.

    ``port`` is anything with pyserial's ``write(bytes)``, ``read(size) -> bytes``
    (returning early on the port's own short timeout, which bounds how quickly a
    deadline or cancellation is noticed) and ``close()``. ``quiet_s`` is how long
    a receive waits for its first byte before answering that nothing was offered.
    """

    def __init__(self, port: Any, *, writer: Any = None, evidence_path: Path | None = None,
                 max_frame_bytes: int = 4096, quiet_s: float = 0.1) -> None:
        self._port = port
        self._writer = writer if writer is not None else StandaloneCaptureWriter()
        self._evidence_path = evidence_path
        self._max_frame = max_frame_bytes
        self._quiet_s = quiet_s
        self._pending = bytearray()  # read from the port, not yet returned
        self._closed = False
        self.evidence: list[dict[str, Any]] = []

    # clocks
    def monotonic(self) -> float:
        return time.monotonic()

    def utc_now(self) -> str:
        return datetime.now(UTC).isoformat(timespec="milliseconds").replace("+00:00", "Z")

    # transport (OTDP section 8.1 stream transactions)
    def _live(self, context: Any) -> None:
        if context.is_cancelled() or self.monotonic() >= context.deadline_monotonic:
            raise TimeoutError("operation cancelled or expired")
        if self._closed:
            raise ConnectionError("serial port is closed")

    async def transfer(self, transaction: dict[str, Any], context: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
        kind = transaction.get("kind")
        if kind not in _FIELDS or set(transaction) != _FIELDS[kind]:
            raise ValueError(f"not a section 8.1 stream transaction: {sorted(transaction)}")
        receive = None
        if kind != "stream_send":
            receive = self._receive_bounds(transaction)
        if kind != "stream_receive" and not isinstance(transaction["data"], bytes):
            raise ValueError("data must be bytes")
        self._live(context)
        if kind != "stream_receive":
            data = transaction["data"]
            try:
                sent = await asyncio.to_thread(self._port.write, data)
            except OSError as error:
                raise ConnectionError(f"serial write failed: {error}") from error
            # pyserial reports a short count without raising when a pending write
            # is cancelled, or under write_timeout=0. None means the port reports
            # no count (pyserial's own rs485.RS485 and cp2110:// ports).
            if sent is not None and sent != len(data):
                raise ConnectionError(f"serial write reported {sent} of {len(data)} bytes")
            if kind == "stream_send":
                return {}
        return {"data": await self._receive(*receive, context)}

    def _receive_bounds(self, t: dict[str, Any]) -> tuple[int, bytes, int]:
        max_bytes, termination, exact = t["max_bytes"], t["termination"], t["exact_bytes"]
        if not isinstance(max_bytes, int) or isinstance(max_bytes, bool) \
                or not 1 <= max_bytes <= self._max_frame:
            raise ValueError(f"max_bytes must be 1..{self._max_frame}")
        if termination not in _TERMINATORS:  # serial does not support "eom"
            raise ValueError("termination must be 'lf' or 'crlf' on a serial port")
        if exact is not None and (not isinstance(exact, int) or isinstance(exact, bool)
                                  or not 0 <= exact <= max_bytes):
            raise ValueError("exact_bytes must be None or 0..max_bytes")
        return max_bytes, _TERMINATORS[termination], exact or 0

    async def _receive(self, max_bytes: int, terminator: bytes, exact: int, context: Any) -> bytes:
        quiet_until = self.monotonic() + self._quiet_s
        while True:
            if exact:  # a positive exact_bytes takes precedence over termination
                if len(self._pending) >= exact:
                    return self._take(exact)
            else:
                end = self._pending[:max_bytes].find(terminator)
                if end >= 0:
                    return self._take(end + len(terminator))
                if len(self._pending) >= max_bytes:
                    self._take(max_bytes)  # discard, so the next call can resynchronise
                    raise ValueError(f"no terminator within {max_bytes} bytes")
            if not self._pending and self.monotonic() >= quiet_until:
                return b""  # nothing offered: a quiet line, not an error
            self._live(context)  # a partial frame stays pending across the timeout
            want = (exact or max_bytes) - len(self._pending)
            try:
                chunk = await asyncio.to_thread(self._port.read, max(1, want))
            except OSError as error:
                raise ConnectionError(f"serial read failed: {error}") from error
            self._pending += chunk

    def _take(self, count: int) -> bytes:
        out = bytes(self._pending[:count])
        del self._pending[:count]
        return out

    async def close_transport(self, context: Any) -> None:
        if not self._closed:
            self._closed = True
            await asyncio.to_thread(self._port.close)

    # evidence
    async def record_evidence(self, entry: dict[str, Any], context: Any) -> None:
        record = {**entry, "at": self.utc_now(), "operation_id": context.operation_id}
        self.evidence.append(record)
        if self._evidence_path is not None:
            with self._evidence_path.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as stream:
                stream.write(json.dumps(record, sort_keys=True) + "\n")

    # capture: the SDK's standalone writer
    async def artifact_append(self, capture_id: str, data: bytes, context: Any) -> None:
        await self._writer.artifact_append(capture_id, data, context)

    async def artifact_finalise(self, capture_id: str, metadata: dict[str, Any],
                                context: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return await self._writer.artifact_finalise(capture_id, metadata, context)

    async def artifact_abort(self, capture_id: str) -> None:
        await self._writer.artifact_abort(capture_id)
```

Using it with pyserial and a plugin's adapter:

```python
import serial  # pyserial, installed separately

port = serial.Serial("/dev/ttyUSB0", 115200, timeout=0.05)
host = SerialStandaloneHost(port, writer=StandaloneCaptureWriter(formats=("raw_binary",)))
plugin = create_plugin()
open_context = BenchContext("open", timeout_s=2.0)
await plugin.open(descriptor, host, open_context)
op_context = BenchContext("bench-1", timeout_s=2.0)
result = await plugin.execute({"operation_id": "bench-1", "verb": "read",
                               "arguments": {"parameter": "voltage"}}, op_context)
```

Give each operation its own `BenchContext`. The adapter checks `operation_id` against the request. `tests/test_guide_serial_host.py` executes the first block above and drives a freshly scaffolded plugin through it, so the example cannot drift from the SDK or from the generated adapter.

### Reconfigure the serial link at runtime

Some devices switch their line speed without a reconnect. The descriptor declares this with `x-negotiated-bauds` under `transport.settings`. The value is a list of baud rates the adapter may switch to. The boot baud is always allowed. Without the declaration, every switch refuses. The capability is opt-in by design.

The host checks the declaration when the session builds. A malformed value stops the build with a clear error. The host adds no range rules. Which baud rates a bench may use is the descriptor author's decision.

The serial host in the SDK server serves this capability. An adapter detects it with `hasattr(services, "reconfigure_link")`. A host without the capability hands adapters plain `HostServices`. One switch request carries exactly `{"baud": <int>}`. Parity, stop bits, data bits and flow control stay at their boot settings. A request with any other field refuses.

A switch is one bounded attempt:

1. The host refuses the request while a receive is in flight.
2. The host closes the old link. The old ring dies with it. Bytes that arrived at the old baud are not frames at the new one, so the new link starts empty.
3. The host reopens the port at the boot settings, with the new baud in place.
4. The host returns the applied settings. This read-back is the proof.

The host never retries a failed switch. A failed reopen leaves no serving link and raises `ConnectionError`. The adapter may then request the boot baud as its own explicit step. That is the adapter's move.

`host_info` and `device_get` carry a `link` block on the serial transport: the current baud, the boot baud, and whether any switch is negotiable. The block is `null` on other transports and before a connection. The event stream carries the `link` family. Each event says what happened (`reconfigured`, `reconfigure_refused` or `reconfigure_failed`), both baud rates, and the operation id.
### Capture retention and the library page (standalone host)

The standalone host adds retention, a storage reserve and a library page over one capture root. A retention rules document states what the host keeps and what it removes. The document is a JSON file with an explicit path. Its top-level keys are `interval_s`, `orphan_grace_s`, `reserve_bytes` and `rules`, and every key is optional. Each rule has a unique, non-empty `id`. A rule can carry the match keys `source` (`ui`, `rest` or `mcp`) and `project` (an exact string). An absent match key matches anything.

Each rule needs at least one limit. `max_age_d` removes captures strictly older than the given number of days. `max_count` keeps only the newest N captures. `max_bytes` keeps only the newest prefix that fits. Without a document, the shipped ruled defaults apply: mcp captures are kept 30 days unless pinned, and ui and rest captures are kept until you delete them. The defaults ship as a document inside the package (`retention-defaults.json`), not as host constants. A custom document does not replace the defaults. The document's rules are added on top of the defaults, and a custom rule id must not equal the default id `default-mcp-30d`.

```json
{
  "interval_s": 86400,
  "orphan_grace_s": 900,
  "reserve_bytes": 2000000000,
  "rules": [
    {"id": "ui-age-30d", "source": "ui", "max_age_d": 30},
    {"id": "rest-keep-200", "source": "rest", "max_count": 200}
  ]
}
```

The CLI command `benchweave-sdk-server prune` applies the rules from outside the host: the shipped defaults when no document is given, or the document's rules added on top of the defaults. The command is root-scoped; it takes no project argument. `--capture-root <path>` names the capture root. `--retention-rules <path>` names the rules document. `--dry-run` lists each removal and its rule, and changes nothing. `--json` emits `{"removals": [...], "summary": {count, bytes}}`.

```sh
benchweave-sdk-server prune --capture-root /path/to/captures --retention-rules rules.json --dry-run
```

The prune removes exactly the plan. Each removal deletes the capture directory and its index row together. The prune also runs the orphan sweep. The sweep removes crash-left directories, which have no `manifest.json`, past the grace window of 900 s by default. A malformed rules document refuses with the `standalone_retention_rules_invalid:` prefix and exit 2. The library's one-writer lock refuses a prune while a host serves the same root: `standalone_library_locked`, exit 2. Stop the host, or use the in-host schedule.

`serve` always runs the same evaluator inside the host on one schedule task. Without a document, the task evaluates the shipped defaults. With `--retention-rules <path>`, the task evaluates the document's rules added on top of the defaults, every `interval_s`, 86400 s by default, over the host's own capture root. The armed capture is excluded. Every run publishes one `retention_pruned` event. For every `max_bytes` rule whose usage crosses 0.8 rising, the host publishes a `retention_quota` event. A rule already above the threshold fires once, and a rule that drops below and crosses again fires again.

`reserve_bytes` in the same document arms the storage guard. There is no default reserve; each bench commissions its own number. At capture start, the host refuses `unavailable` with the `standalone_storage_reserve:` prefix when the worst case cannot be cleared against the reserve. A duration-bound capture with no byte reservation refuses the same way; declare `max_bytes` for it. During a capture, the host samples free space about every second. On a breach, the host stops the capture and publishes it with `stop_reason: "reserve"` and the real staged byte count. Nothing is discarded silently.

Every removal is appended to `retention.log`, a JSONL file in the capture root. Each row carries the capture id, the manifest's own sha256, the rule, the time and the trigger. The trigger names who removed the capture: the schedule, the CLI, the sweep or a delete. A swept orphan is logged under the rule `orphan-sweep` with a `null` sha256. On exit, through an interrupt or a terminal close, a capture in flight is settled honestly. It is published with its real bytes, or aborted with nothing half-written. No half-written primary files remain.

The host serves the capture library at `GET /captures`. The table shows the capture id, started, format, bytes, source, project, tags, `pinned`, stop reason and the next retention effect. The next-effect column comes from the same evaluator the prune runs: `prunable now by <rule>`, `<rule> at <date>`, `eligible under <rule>` or `kept`. Filters cover project, source, tag, device and free text over id and notes; the device filter reads each capture's metadata file. Pin and unpin are form buttons, and a pinned capture refuses deletion until you unpin it. Delete is a two-step confirmation page that names the capture id, its size and its project. The confirmed delete dispatches through the operations seam and writes its own `retention.log` row with trigger `delete-ui`.

## 4. Review compatibility and deployment

Use the [AI device integration reviewer](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave/blob/main/docs/ai-device-reviewer.md) (main repository) with the exact revision and test evidence. Its SDK maintenance checklist covers public interfaces, contracts, generated projects, mocks, gateway compatibility and release artefacts.

The gateway now has an explicit `load_otdp_plugin` and `OTDPBridge` path for async adapter API 1.1. The bridge mediates the OTDP verbs `identify`, `read`, `write`, `capture`, `stream_subscribe`, `stream_unsubscribe` and `invoke`: scalar read, scalar write, single-channel capture, streaming subscriptions and pinned-contract invoke. The `capture` verb comes with pre-dispatch bounds checks, staged appends and a host-computed manifest. The step's `timeout_ms` is the capture budget. The release smoke exercises a generated multi-module plugin through identify and read. Separate bridge tests cover write conversion and rejection paths. The OTDP loader path also serves dataset publishing and payload services. The bridge does not mediate the `self_test`, `get_errors` and `reset` verbs. Profile scheduling needs a native asynchronous host. The bridge does not supply it. The gateway retains the existing simulator loader for its separate synchronous interface.

A gateway integrator must first do four things:

- complete admission;
- supply the verified manifest and cache, and the descriptor;
- inject authorised scoped services;
- use the same monotonic timebase as the host's deadlines.

The loader rechecks all listed file hashes and imports verified package code and resources in memory. This is an integrity check and namespace isolation, not an operating-system sandbox. Adapters remain trusted Python.

An SDK install does **not** add a plugin to a running workbench. There is no live device-install endpoint, automatic dependency installer or Docker hot-install command. A Docker deployment still needs persistent storage for verified packages, bench configuration, commissioned host services and activation at an approved idle boundary. See [package formats and gateway installation](https://github.com/madeinoz67/benchweave/blob/main/docs/develop-your-device.md#package-format-and-gateway-installation) (main repository).

## 5. Prepare the release, then approve publication

A Python wheel or source distribution and a registry release are different artefacts. Prepare the registry-required identity, exact compatibility, payload inventory, hashes, dependency locks, licence, source and build provenance, SBOM (software bill of materials) and evidence status. [`benchweave-sdk inventory <prepared-bundle-directory>`](../reference/cli/inventory.qmd) prints file paths, byte counts and SHA-256 values. It does not create or approve a complete registry manifest.

Before you publish, show the owner the actual built files, the evidence and the remaining gaps. Hardware qualification and local commissioning remain separate. The SDK retains the project's proprietary licence declaration. Release owners must establish distribution rights before they share it publicly.

After your submission lands as a pull request (PR), track it without asking anyone. `benchweave-sdk registry status --publisher <you> --registry-clone <clone-of-benchweave-registry>` reports your exact submission set. It also reports every release's lifecycle timeline, from the committed records alone. The timeline covers publishes, advisories, yanks and transfers. This command is the contributor-facing half of the queue that maintainers see. Stages carry `stage_partial` flags, because PR-side review activity is not derivable from records. The maintainer's `registry queue` reads it when a live `gh` is available.

## Maintenance and release cycle

The main repository's Package workflow builds the gateway and SDK from source distributions, then tests installed wheels in temporary environments on Linux and macOS. It generates, builds and installs an external plugin outside the checkout. It runs the plugin's tests. It checks packaged contract bytes and versions. It exercises gateway loading. It rejects tampered code.

Run the same check locally from a checkout of the main BenchWeave repository. The script `scripts/sdk_smoke.py` lives there, not in this repository. Run:

```sh
uv run --no-project --python 3.13 scripts/sdk_smoke.py --out-dir dist/packages
```

On a published GitHub release, a separate job repeats these checks. It then attaches the SDK wheel and source distribution to that release. A release tag triggers the publish workflow. The workflow builds the source distribution and wheel. It smoke-installs the wheel on five OS and arch lanes (Linux x86-64 and arm64, macOS arm64 and Intel, and Windows). It verifies each installed wheel's vendored standards with `benchweave-sdk sync-standards --check`. It publishes to PyPI via Trusted Publishing. No release is published simply by an edit to these files or by a run of the local smoke check.

An installed SDK can verify its own vendored standards offline: `benchweave-sdk sync-standards --check` compares the packaged lock with the packaged tree and needs no repository checkout. An import of a standards bundle rewrites the source tree, so the command refuses to run outside a checkout (`sync_requires_repo_checkout:`).

When you change the SDK API, canonical contracts, template, gateway bridge or build tooling, update the affected tests and documentation together. Keep SDK distribution metadata, `__version__`, generated development dependency and this compatibility statement aligned. The smoke checks guard the installed distribution and contract resources.
